name: Jawaharlal Nehru
info: Jawaharlal Nehru was an Indian lawyer, nationalist and statesman, a principal leader of the independence movement and India's first prime minister from 1947 until his death in 1964, remembered for parliamentary democracy, secularism and non-alignment.

facts.born: 14 November 1889, in Allahabad in British India; first child of the barrister and Congress leader Motilal Nehru and Swarup Rani, of the Kashmiri Pandit community
facts.died: 27 May 1964, in office, of what was believed to be a heart attack; cremated by Hindu rites at the Shantivan on the banks of the Yamuna
facts.role: Barrister of the Allahabad High Court (from 1912); general secretary and several times president of the Indian National Congress (president from 1929); interim prime minister (1946-1947); first Prime Minister of India (1947-1964), holding External Affairs throughout
facts.known: The Lahore resolution for complete independence (1929); the "Tryst with Destiny" speech; parliamentary democracy and secularism; planned industrialisation and a mixed economy; the Indian Institutes of Technology and other institutions; the Non-Aligned Movement; the Sino-Indian War of 1962; The Discovery of India and An Autobiography

t: Educated at Harrow and Cambridge, Nehru gave up the law for the nationalist movement, spent over nine years in British prisons and became, with Gandhi's backing, the leader who called for complete independence in 1929.

As India's first prime minister for nearly seventeen years he promoted parliamentary democracy, secularism, science and planned industrialisation, and led the Non-Aligned Movement between the Cold War blocs.
His reputation suffered from India's defeat in the 1962 war with China, and critics fault his economic protectionism, his handling of Kashmir and what they call his selective secularism.
dyk: Nehru's best-known books, among them The Discovery of India, Glimpses of World History and An Autobiography, were all written in jail; Letters from a Father to His Daughter was written to Indira, then ten years old.
ev: Jawaharlal Nehru is born in Allahabad, the son of the barrister Motilal Nehru
He is imprisoned for anti-government activity, the first of eight detentions up to 1945
As Congress president at Lahore he carries the resolution for complete independence
After the Quit India resolution he is arrested with the Congress working committee
He becomes the first prime minister of independent India and gives the "Tryst with Destiny" speech
He is a key organiser of the Bandung Conference of newly independent nations from Asia and Africa
Nehru dies in office and is succeeded by Lal Bahadur Shastri

sections.early:
Jawaharlal Nehru was born on 14 November 1889 in Allahabad in British India, the first child of Swarup Rani and Motilal Nehru. Both parents belonged to the community of Kashmiri Pandits. Motilal was a self-made barrister of wealth who served twice as president of the Indian National Congress; of Jawaharlal's two younger sisters, Vijaya Lakshmi became the first woman president of the United Nations General Assembly. Nehru called his childhood "sheltered and uneventful", spent in the mansion Anand Bhavan and taught at home. A tutor, Ferdinand T. Brooks, drew him to theosophy, and Annie Besant initiated him into the Theosophical Society at thirteen; through it he first studied the Buddhist and Hindu scriptures.

The Russo-Japanese War stirred his nationalism: he "mused of Indian freedom and Asiatic freedom from the thraldom of Europe". At Harrow from 1905 he was inspired by G. M. Trevelyan's books on Garibaldi. He went to Trinity College, Cambridge, in October 1907, took an honours degree in natural science in 1910, and read Shaw, Wells, Keynes and Russell. He studied law at the Inner Temple and was called to the Bar in 1912. Back in India that August he enrolled at the Allahabad High Court, but he relished neither the law nor the company of lawyers. In 1916 he married Kamala Kaul; their only daughter, Indira, was born in 1917.
sections.rise:
Nehru sympathised with the Congress radicals rather than his father's moderates, and in 1916 joined the Home Rule Leagues, becoming secretary of Annie Besant's. He first met Gandhi that year, and after the Jallianwala Bagh killings of 1919 father and son accepted Gandhi's methods. During the non-cooperation movement he directed political activity in the United Provinces, and on 6 December 1921 was imprisoned, the first of eight detentions between 1921 and 1945 that lasted over nine years in all. By 1923 he was general secretary of the Congress and mayor of Allahabad. A visit to the Soviet Union in 1927 drew him to socialism, though he never fully agreed with Marx.

He was one of the first leaders to demand a complete break with the British Empire. On 29 December 1929 he became Congress president at Lahore and carried a resolution for complete independence, and at midnight on New Year's Eve he hoisted the tricolour on the banks of the Ravi. After Lahore he gradually emerged as the paramount leader of the movement, and Gandhi in 1942 named him his political heir. He was jailed again during the salt satyagraha of 1930 and in the 1930s; in 1933 the government called him "by far the most dangerous element at large in India". His wife Kamala died in Switzerland in February 1936. He led the Congress campaign in the 1937 provincial elections and, after the Quit India resolution of 8 August 1942, was imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort until June 1945.
sections.deeds:
Nehru became interim prime minister in September 1946 and, at independence on 15 August 1947, prime minister of India, opening with his "Tryst with Destiny" speech. With Vallabhbhai Patel he oversaw the integration of the princely states, and he moved the Objectives Resolution that became the Preamble of the Constitution, which made India a republic on 26 January 1950. The Congress under him won the elections of 1951-52, 1957 and 1962.

He favoured a mixed economy of public and private sectors and import substitution, directing investment into steel, iron, coal and power. Industry grew 7.0% a year between 1950 and 1965, almost trebling output and making India the world's seventh-largest industrial country, while GDP grew at about 3.9% a year. A land reform abolished giant landholdings, and agricultural universities prepared the way for the Green Revolution. His government founded the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, the Indian Institutes of Technology and the Indian Institutes of Management, and the Hindu code bills of 1955-56 criminalised caste discrimination and widened women's legal rights.

Holding External Affairs throughout, he kept India in the Commonwealth as a republic, signed the Panchsheel with China in 1954, helped organise the Bandung Conference of 1955 and was a key participant in the first Non-Aligned summit at Belgrade in 1961. He campaigned for the abolition of what he called "these frightful engines of destruction".
sections.opponents:
Nehru's foreign record drew the sharpest criticism. From 1959 his "Forward Policy" set up military outposts in disputed border areas, 43 of them in territory India had not previously controlled; China attacked, and India lost the war of 1962. It exposed an army that could send only 14,000 troops to the front, and Nehru was widely criticised for neglecting defence; his defence minister, V. K. Krishna Menon, resigned. On Kashmir he had promised a plebiscite under the United Nations in 1948 but declined to hold it in 1953, when he also orchestrated the ouster and arrest of the Kashmiri prime minister Sheikh Abdullah. Though averse to war, he used military force to annex Hyderabad in 1948 and Goa in 1961, for which the communist opposition criticised him.

At home, critics argued that his import substitution weakened the competitiveness of Indian manufacturing, and growth was considered anaemic beside the economies of Japan and Western Europe. Bhikhu Parekh, who calls him the founder of the modern Indian state, judges that his policies failed to benefit the urban and rural poor and the unemployed. Because he left Muslim personal law unreformed while reforming Hindu law, he has been accused of selective secularism, and his secularist policies remain debated, mainly by Hindutva proponents. Morarji Desai later alleged that he used the Kamaraj Plan of 1963 to clear the way for his daughter, and Indira's election as Congress president in 1959 drew charges of nepotism, though Nehru disapproved of it.
sections.last:
Patel's death in 1950 had left Nehru the unchallenged leader of India, and he was at the peak of his popularity in the late 1950s. His health declined steadily from 1962: he spent most of April that year in bed with a viral infection and months of 1963 recuperating in Kashmir. Some writers attribute the decline to his chagrin over the war with China, which he saw as a betrayal of trust. In 1963 he brought in legislation making it illegal to demand secession, and the Official Languages Act to ensure the use of English beyond 1965. Indira had moved into his residence and become in effect his chief of staff.

He survived several attempts on his life, among them a knife attack near Nagpur in 1955 and a failed bombing of train tracks in Maharashtra in 1961, and he disliked heavy security. Returning from Dehradun on 26 May 1964 he went to bed as usual; early the next morning he complained of pain in the back, collapsed almost at once and died at 13:44 on 27 May without regaining consciousness. The cause was believed to be a heart attack. Parliament was told, in words like his own at Gandhi's death, "The light is out." On 28 May he was cremated by Hindu rites at the Shantivan on the Yamuna before 1.5 million mourners, although his will had asked that no religious ceremonies be performed. He left no clear political heir, and Lal Bahadur Shastri succeeded him.
sections.legacy:
Next to Gandhi, Nehru is regarded as the most significant figure of the Indian independence movement, and on the first anniversary of his death Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, Lal Bahadur Shastri and others called him the greatest figure of modern India after Gandhi. Called an "architect of India", he shaped the country's government, political culture and foreign policy; he is credited with keeping India together against predictions that it would fall apart, with a system of universal primary education and with the institutions of higher learning founded under him. He popularised "unity in diversity" as state policy and set up the National Book Trust and the National Literary Academy to carry regional literature between languages.

His birthday, 14 November, is celebrated as Children's Day, and children remember him as Chacha Nehru. The Jawaharlal Nehru University, the Nehru Memorial Museum & Library at Teen Murti House and the family homes at Anand Bhavan are among his memorials. His ideals still shape the Congress Party's manifesto. Writing in 2005, Ramachandra Guha judged that had Nehru died in 1958 he would be remembered as the greatest statesman of the 20th century. His books were widely read: Michael Brecher found Glimpses of World History polemical but of great artistic value, and The Guardian rated "Tryst with Destiny" among the great speeches of the century.

summary: Jawaharlal Nehru, born in Allahabad in 1889, became a leader of the Indian National Congress, demanded complete independence in 1929 and spent years in British prisons. As India's first prime minister from 1947 to 1964 he built a secular parliamentary republic, planned industry and led non-alignment, while the 1962 war with China damaged his standing.
references: Sarvepalli Gopal, Jawaharlal Nehru: A Biography, Volume 1 1889–1947 (Oxford University Press, 1976)
Jeffrey Kopstein, Comparative Politics: Interests, Identities, and Institutions in a Changing Global Order (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
B.R. Nanda, The Nehrus: Motilal and Jawaharlal (Oxford University Press, 2007)
B. Stein, A History of India (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010)

notes: Term of office: the lead says '16 years and 286 days' (from 15 August 1947); a later section says 'nearly eighteen years' counting the interim government. I wrote 'nearly seventeen years' in a takeaway, which matches the first; the editor may prefer to drop the figure.
Gandhi named Nehru his heir 'explicitly' in 1942 per one passage, while a 15 January 1941 statement already says 'Jawaharlal will be my successor'. I followed the article's sentence giving 1942.
The 1962 war: the article says Menon 'resigned' (in quotation marks once); I wrote 'resigned'.

Partition and its violence: the article mentions only 'outbreaks of communal violence' in early 1947 and gives no figures; I did not address partition beyond that, as the article says little of Nehru's role in it.
The 200,000 arrests after Gandhi's death (RSS, Muslim National Guards, Khaksars) are in the article, attributed to Nehru and Patel; left out for space.

Wanted but not in the article: casualty figures for the 1962 war; detail on partition violence and refugees; the CIA plot of 1955 is stated flatly in the article and I left it out as unsourced in the text.
